source.title: A theory of platonic representations in language models
source.authors: Darshil Doshi; Wen-Jie Zhou; C. Wegner; D. Korchinski; Santiago Acevedo; M. Wyart

record.file_problem: No apparent truncation or garbling; the full paper and appendices are present.
record.tranche_reason: The paper tests cross-lingual representational similarity and refines the convergence account: similarity is incomplete, varies with language structure and data exposure, and is distinct from coordinate alignment.
record.gate_note: Rows below are the paper's own measurements and explicit reported outcomes. The figures give many results without exact numeric values, so those values are recorded as figure only. Results cited from other work, including the adapted multilingual-LLM result in Fig. 4(d), are not rows. The paper discusses cross-modal convergence as a possible extension but does not test vision-language representations.
record.test_reason: Two independently initialized 8-layer transformers, trained separately on two synthetic languages, are compared with II and mKNN on translation pairs (Fig. 2c,d). These are convergence measurements between separately trained models. They show similarity that is incomplete, depends on layer, varies with how much hierarchy the languages share, and is consistent across the two metrics. This bears on V6 and V7. The paper also offers a theory that restates convergence as geometric similarity distinct from coordinate alignment. Most other results are within a single multilingual model, which no version names.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors argue that a hidden hierarchy, with shared abstract levels and language-specific surface levels, explains the main facts. These are: cross-lingual similarity peaks in middle layers, coexists with language-specific structure, and grows with language proximity, model quality and data exposure. Coordinate alignment is distinct from similarity and requires code-switched data. The record omits two things the authors stress. Their theory predicts that layerwise novelty increases cross-lingual similarity, which they confirm in pretrained LLMs. They also suggest, without testing, that the analysis extends to cross-modal convergence.
record.recipe_differences: Uses synthetic multilingual grammars, BP theory, and II/mKNN to study cross-lingual language representations; it does not reproduce the original cross-modal model-scale comparison.
record.method_sensitivity: Similarity changes with shared versus surface hierarchy, language-specific data exposure, layer depth, and whether raw representations or layerwise novelty are measured. II and mKNN are reported to give consistent qualitative trends. The paper fixes mKNN k=10 rather than sweeping k.

fits_no_version.finding: Within one multilingual transformer, translation-pair representations are most similar in middle layers and less similar for more distant languages. The same holds in Mistral-7B, OLMo-3-7B and EuroLLM-9B on Europarl.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Within-model cross-lingual convergence: a single multilingual model represents translations similarly in middle layers, more so for closer languages.

fits_no_version.finding: Within-model cross-lingual similarity grows with training-set size and next-token performance. It weakens as one language's share of training data shrinks.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Within-model cross-lingual similarity scales with model quality and per-language data exposure.

fits_no_version.finding: Subtracting the component affinely predictable from the previous layer lowers cross-lingual II at intermediate layers, in the synthetic models and in 7-9B LLMs.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Layerwise residual (novelty) representations expose more cross-lingual similarity than raw hidden states.

fits_no_version.finding: A linear probe trained on one language transfers to the other only with code-switched training data (threshold P ∝ 1/ϵ). With ϵ=0, more data yields geometric similarity but no coordinate alignment.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Geometric similarity across languages does not imply shared coordinates; alignment requires cross-lingual training signal.

record.problems: The controlled transformer experiments use synthetic MRHM grammars, two languages, and a fixed transformer architecture. Several key plotted results are not numerically reported in the text. The paper does not test cross-modal convergence, broad architectural/objective variation, or out-of-distribution robustness; it states that its framework extension to joint-embedding methods is future work.
record.rows_left_out: The appendix contains additional figure-based curves and comparisons for BP decay settings, parsimonious BP, varying transformer depth and topology, residual/supra-word novelty baselines, and further natural-language model/language-pair combinations (Figs. 10-19). These were not individually extracted to keep the record focused on the primary claim-relevant outcomes; the natural-language novelty findings are represented by R19-R21 and the main text reports the broader result.

untested.parts: No variation of model size or capability across independently trained models. The P-scaling result (Fig. 3) is within a single model.
No vision-language models or image-caption pairs; cross-modal extension is only argued.
Separately trained models differ in training language as well as seed; no same-data, different-seed comparison.
No mapping, stitching or relative representations between separate models. Cross-probing is within one model.
No neuron, SAE-feature or circuit comparison across models.
No sweep of k or N, no global metrics such as CKA (only cited), no out-of-distribution inputs for cross-model comparisons.

Causes are not isolated. The separate models share architecture and objective, and their languages share a latent hierarchy, so shared objective cannot be separated from shared latent structure. No plateau test across separate models.

missing.what: Cross-model II and mKNN profiles for independently trained models at ϵ=0, highest P; better fit by encoder-only BP.
Explicit statement that raw mKNN values depend on k and on evaluation-set size N (chance ≈ k/(N-1)); comparisons valid only at fixed N, k.
Cross-model similarity as a function of training-set size P, if any. The text reports P-scaling only for Fig. 3, which appears to be within-model; this needs checking.

record.verdict_notes: The paper is framed around the Platonic hypothesis, but most results measure cross-lingual similarity within one model, which no version names; I set those rows to none and listed them under fits_no_version. Only Fig. 2(c,d), with separate models trained on different languages, measures between-model convergence. No numeric values are given; all results are figure-only and averaged over 4 seeds without error bars. The theory attributes similarity to shared latent generative structure in the data. In this synthetic setup that structure is the ground truth, so it could be read as a 'common model of reality' rather than shared data. Shared objective and architecture are not varied, so V7's causal part stays untested. The V6 challenge is narrow: it covers agreement between two local metrics only. The paper cites other work finding that global metrics like CKA give weaker support.

versions.untested_parts: Tests similarity as training data and next-token performance improve in a fixed synthetic-model setup; does not vary model size or compare models with different architectures, objectives, or modalities.
No vision-language model representations of paired images and captions are measured.

Does not test shared features or subspaces across same-architecture models trained from different seeds on the same task; independently trained models here are trained on different languages and compared geometrically.

Tests cross-language coordinate compatibility using linear cross-probes in a multilingual model. Does not test mapping representations between separate models, stitching, relative representations, or alignment without paired data.
Does not test recurrence of interpretable neurons, SAE features, or circuits across models.
Tests dependence on shared hierarchical structure, language exposure, and two similarity metrics (II and mKNN). Does not sweep the mKNN neighbor count or test out-of-distribution inputs.

Tests incomplete geometric similarity and the role of shared hierarchy and code-switched training signal in its synthetic language setting. Does not isolate shared real-world pretraining data or objectives as causes in independently trained natural-language models.
